reviewer: Codex manual inspection of all 70 raw patient replies
summary: Both candidate LLMs produced clinically unauthorized additions or patient-role failures.
rationale: The zero-unauthorized-facts requirement cannot be approved from lexical checks alone. Manual inspection found material failures in both models even after raw learner text was removed from the phrasing prompt.
concerns: Qwen3 1.7B frequently adopted clinician/assistant language, exposed response-planning language, used third person, or generated malformed and truncated replies.
Qwen3 4B was more natural but invented symptoms, negative findings, prior medication context, work details, recovery timing, and symptom changes that the controller did not authorize.
Neither tested model can currently be trusted as a free-form phrasing layer under the zero-unauthorized-facts acceptance criterion.
The 30-token minimum is poorly matched to brief patient answers and encourages filler; retain a 60-token maximum and evaluate natural minimum length by plan type instead.

representativeFindings.detail: Produced analysis text beginning 'Okay, let's see' instead of a patient reply.
Said it wanted to support the learner and discuss ways to manage symptoms.
Invented a need to make money while waiting.
Refused medical advice and referred the learner to a healthcare professional.
Apologized for dismissing the learner and offered further help.
Said it needed to clarify its response plan.
Referred to the patient as 'he' instead of speaking in first person.
Tried to redirect constructively and asked how it could assist.
Invented shakiness, lightheadedness, and symptom tracking.
Claimed there were no other symptoms.
Invented uncertainty about whether the medicine worked and implied a prior medicine.
Introduced standing as a trigger even though only onset was authorized.
Added being alone and not wanting to rely on others.
Invented full-time work status and a return-to-work date next week.
Invented stiffness and characterized the injury as not too bad.
